titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §§279–280: Ögödei's relay posts and the levy of sheep
part: §§279–280 — Ögödei's relay posts and the levy of sheep
about: Ögödei Qahan lays down how the realm is to bear its own weight: a yearly levy of sheep for the Qahan's table, with a share set aside for the poor; guards and stores; wells in the land of Chül; and a chain of post-stations, with grooms and fixed numbers of oxen, carts and mares, enforced by harsh penalties. Cha'adai is consulted by messenger and undertakes to have Batu told, and the princes and officers assent.

sentences.t: Basa Ögödei Qaγan ügülerün:
sentences.l: Again, Ögödei Qaγan, saying:
sentences.i: Again Ögödei Qahan spoke:
sentences.n: Basa “again” (Ming 再) opens the section as a continuation of the preceding story. Ügülerün is ügüle- “speak” with the converb of time -rün, “while saying” (Ming 說), the usual way the text brings in a speech. Shiratori puts the opening quotation mark at the next word, Čiṅgis; the speech it opens runs all through §279 and closes at boltuγai.

morph.gloss: Ögödei — Ögödei, a man's name (personal name) [(人)名]

sentences.t: "Čiṅgis Qaγan ečige-jüġen žoban baiγ̇uluγsan ulus-i bu žoboγ̇aja.
sentences.l: "Čiṅgis Qaγan one's-own-father toil having-set-up people-(obj) not let-us-trouble.
sentences.i: “Let us not burden the people whom my father Chinggis Qahan established with toil.
sentences.n: Read ečige-jüġen as ečige “father” + the reflexive-possessive -jüġen, “one's own father” (Ming 父 自的行); the “own” points back to the speaker, so “my father”. Baiγ̇uluγsan is bai- “stand” + causative -γ̇ul- + participle -γsan, “that was set up” (Ming 立了的); žoban “toil” is the manner, “with toil”. Bu … -ja is the prohibitive “do not” with the hortative -ja, “let us not trouble” (Ming 休 … 敎辛苦咱). The stem žoboγ̇a- is inferred from the Ming 敎 “cause”; the reading is uncertain.

morph.gloss: Čiṅgis — Chinggis, the title borne by Temüjin from 1206 [太祖︀]
bai- — to stand, be (verb); with the causative, 'set up' [立了的]
žoboγ̇a- — to trouble, cause hardship (stem inferred from žoban and the Ming 敎 'cause'; uncertain) (verb) [敎辛苦]
hortative: 'let us …' (first person plural, back-vowel form)

sentences.t: Köl an-u köser-e γar an-u γažar-a talbiγ̇ulžu žirγaγ̇uluja.
sentences.l: Foot their ground-on, hand their land-on, making-set-down, let-us-make-glad.
sentences.i: Having their feet set down on the ground and their hands on the land, let us make them glad.
sentences.n: An-u is the third-person genitive set after its noun: köl an-u “their foot”, γar an-u “their hand” (Ming 他的). Köser-e and γažar-a are dative-locatives, “on the ground”, “on the land” (Ming 行); the stem köser is inferred from the Ming 地. Talbiγ̇ulžu is talbi- “set down” + causative + converb (Ming 敎放着). Žirγaγ̇uluja is žirγa- “be glad” + causative -γ̇ul- + hortative -ja (Ming 敎快活咱). The first part is a converb (“having had them set down”), not a wish; the only verb of will is žirγaγ̇uluja. The feet and hands at rest I take as a figure for living in peace; that is my reading of the sense, not the Ming's wording.

morph.gloss: an-u — their (third-person genitive placed after its noun) [他的]
köser — ground, earth (noun; stem read from the Ming) [地行]
an-u — their (third-person genitive placed after its noun) [他的]
talbi- — to set down, let go (verb) [敎放着]
žirγa- — to be glad, rejoice (stem inferred from žirγalaṅ) (verb) [敎快活咱]

sentences.t: Qaγan ečige-jüġen belen-dür saγ̇užu irge ülü žoboγ̇an
sentences.l: Qaγan one's-own-father ready-in sitting, people not troubling,
sentences.i: Sitting in the ready-made realm of my father the Qahan, and not troubling the people,
sentences.n: The Ming gloss at ečige-jüġen here reads 人 “person” where the same word above has 父 “father”; I take it as a slip for 父. Whether Qaγan ečige-jüġen means “my father the Qahan” or Ögödei himself as the Qahan is open; I read the first, as in the previous sentence. Belen-dür (Ming 見成裏) is “in what is ready-made”, which I take to be the realm Chinggis had already built (“realm” is my supply; there is no genitive, only the nouns side by side). Irge here is “people” (Ming 百姓), a form of irgen, not the “wether” of §280. Ülü žoboγ̇an is ülü “not” + the converb of žoboγ̇a-. The chain running to ögtügei is broken here for reading; Shiratori has only the full stop at ögtügei.

morph.gloss: ečige — father (noun; the Ming here reads 人 'person', evidently a slip for 父) [人 自的行]
irge — people (a form of irgen; Ming 百姓) [百姓]
ülü — not (negates a converb or participle) [不]
žoboγ̇a- — to trouble, cause hardship (stem inferred; uncertain) (verb) [敎辛苦]

sentences.t: sülen-e ede ulus-ača sürüg-ün nigen šilekü qonin hon hon-dur ögtügei.
sentences.l: Broth-for these people-from herd-of one two-year sheep year year-in let-them-give.
sentences.i: let one two-year-old sheep of the flock be given, for the broth, from these people each year.
sentences.n: Sülen is “soup, broth” (Ming 湯行, “to the broth”); I take it, from the sense, as a levy of animals for the ruler's table, which the Ming does not say. Sürüg-ün nigen šilekü qonin is “one two-year sheep of the herd” (Ming 羣的 一箇 二歲 羊), that is, one from each flock. Hon hon-dur (Ming 年 年裏) is “year, in the year”, that is “each year”. Ulus-ača is the ablative “from these people”: the people are the source of the sheep, and ögtügei is impersonal, “let it be given”. Ögtügei is ög- “give” + the optative -tügei, “let them give” (Ming 與者).

morph.gloss: sülen — soup, broth (noun; here, I think, the levy for the ruler's table) [湯行]
ede — these (plural of ene) (demonstrative pronoun) [這的(每)]
šilekü — two-year-old (of an animal) (adjective; reading from the Ming 二歲) [二歲]

sentences.t: Žaγ̇un qonid-ača nigen qonin γarγažu mün žaγ̇ura ügeġün dutaγ̇un-a ögtügei.
sentences.l: Hundred sheep-from one sheep taking-out, just midway poor lacking-to let-them-give.
sentences.i: From every hundred sheep let one be drawn out, and let it be given, among themselves, to the poor and needy.
sentences.n: Qonid-ača is “from the sheep” with the plural -d; žaγ̇un qonid-ača nigen qonin is “from a hundred sheep, one sheep”. Mün žaγ̇ura (Ming 只 其間) is “just in between, among”; I read “among themselves” (the people), but this is tentative. Ügeġün is ügei “without” + -ġün “those without” (a guess from the Ming 窮 … 的每), and dutaγ̇un-a is “to those lacking” (Ming 乏的行); together “the poor and needy”.

morph.gloss: ügei — without, there is not (negative particle) [窮]
plural: 'those without' (a guess from the Ming 的每)
dutaγ̇u- — to lack, be wanting (verb) [乏的行]

sentences.t: Basa aqa deġü olon ele aγta kešigten čiγ̇uluγ̇asu undan tere tutum irgen-eče ker qubčiγdaqui.
sentences.l: Again elder-brothers younger-brothers many indeed gelding guardsmen if-gathering, drink that each people-from how be-levied.
sentences.i: Again: when my many brothers, elder and younger, and the guardsmen with their geldings gather, how is each such drinking to be levied from the people?
sentences.n: Aqa deġü olon is “elder brothers, younger brothers, many”. Aγta kešigten (Ming 騸馬 護衞每) I read as “guardsmen with geldings”; aγta could also stand apart, “geldings, guardsmen”, so this is tentative. Undan (Ming 飮) is “drink”; tere tutum (Ming 那 每) “each of those times”. Ker … qubčiγdaqui: ker “how”; qubčiγ- “levy” (stem inferred from the Ming 科斂), passive -da-, participle -qui, “is to be levied”. The sentence is a question about how the cost of entertaining is to be met without burdening the people.

morph.gloss: ele — emphatic particle: only, indeed (Ming 但) [但]
kešig — turn of duty, watch (noun) [護衞(每)]
plural possessive: 'those having a turn, guardsmen'
tutum — each, every one (pronoun or adjective) [每]
ker — how, in what manner (interrogative adverb) [怎生]
qubčiγ- — to levy, exact contributions (stem inferred from the Ming 科斂; uncertain) (verb) [可科斂]

sentences.t: Žüg žüg-ün miṅγad miṅγad-ača geġüd γarγažu saγ̇aγ̇ad
sentences.l: Place place-of thousands thousands-from mares taking-out, having-milked
sentences.i: Drawing mares out from the thousands of each region and milking them,
sentences.n: Žüg žüg-ün (Ming 處 各處的) is “place, of each place”, which I read as “each region”; miṅγad-ača is “from the thousands”, the units of a thousand households. Geġüd is geġü “mare kept for milking” + plural -d (Ming (騍)馬每). Γarγažu is γar- “go out” + causative -γa- + converb -žu, “bringing out”. Saγ̇aγ̇ad is saγa- “milk” (Ming 擠) + converb -γ̇ad. This is one sentence with the next unit; I cut it in two for reading.

morph.gloss: geġü — mare kept for milking (noun; Ming (騍)馬每 'mares'; reading uncertain) [(騍)馬每]

sentences.t: saγ̇aričin-tan-i aduγ̇ulaγ̇ad nutučitan-i orošin töled γarγažu unuγ̇učin boltuγai.
sentences.l: their-milkers-(obj) having-herded, their-camp-managers-(obj) constantly replacements taking-out, mare-keepers let-be.
sentences.i: let their milkers be set to herd them, and let the camp-managers regularly bring out replacements, to be the mare-keepers.
sentences.n: The grammar here is uncertain, and so is who becomes the mare-keeper. Saγ̇aričin-tan-i is saγ̇aričin “milker” (Ming 擠馬(的)) + -tan “their, those having” + accusative -i; nutučitan-i is the same for nutuγ̇učin “camp-manager” (printed nutuči-). Aduγ̇ulaγ̇ad (Ming 敎收放了, “have them gathered and put out”) is “having had them herded”. Orošin (Ming 常川) “constantly” and töled (Ming 替頭) “replacements” are both read from the Ming alone. Unuγ̇učin boltuγai is “let them be mare-keepers” (Ming 放乳馬的 做者).

morph.gloss: saγ̇aričin — milker (saγa- 'milk' + agent; read from the Ming 擠馬(的)) [擠馬(的)每行]
aduγ̇ula- — to herd, put to pasture (from aduγ̇un 'herd of horses'; the Ming 敎 'cause' may mean a causative; analysis uncertain) (verb) [敎收放了]
nutuγ — camp, pasture (noun) [管營盤的 行]
orošin — constantly, regularly (adverb; Ming 常川; reading uncertain) [常川]
töle — replacement, substitute (stem inferred from the Ming 替頭) [替頭]
unuγ̇učin — keeper of milk-mares, mare-keeper (Ming 放乳馬的; stem inferred) [放乳馬的]
optative: 'let it be, may it be' (back-vowel form)

sentences.t: Basa aqa deġü čiγ̇uluγ̇asu öglige sojurγal ögüje.
sentences.l: Again elder-brothers younger-brothers if-gathering, reward favour let-us-give.
sentences.i: Again: when my brothers, elder and younger, gather, let us give them rewards and favours.
sentences.n: Čiγ̇uluγ̇asu is čiγul- “gather” + the conditional-temporal -γ̇asu (Ming 聚呵, “when they gather”), the same word as in the feast sentence above. Öglige (Ming 賞) “reward” and sojurγal (Ming 賜) “favour, bounty” are the two gifts; ögüje is ög- “give” + the hortative -üje, “let us give” (Ming 與咱).

morph.gloss: sojurγal — favour, grace, bounty (noun; from sojurγa- 'show favour') [賜]
hortative: 'let us …' (first person plural, front-vowel form)

sentences.t: Aγ̇urasun sükes qod numud qujaγ žebe saṅγ̇ud tüsürčü balaγad sakiγ̇uluγ̇a.
sentences.l: Cloth silver-ingots quivers bows armour weapons granaries pouring, storehouses let-us-have-guarded.
sentences.i: Let us store cloth, silver ingots, quivers, bows, armour and weapons in granaries and treasuries, and have them guarded.
sentences.n: This is a list of goods: aγ̇urasun (Ming 段疋) “bolts of cloth”, sükes (Ming 銀錠) “silver ingots”, qod and numud “quivers” and “bows” (qor, numu + plural -d), qujaγ “armour”, and žebe “weapons” (the common noun, not the name Jebe). Saṅγ̇ud (Ming 倉每) “granaries” has an uncertain stem. Tüsürčü (Ming 注着, “pouring”) I take as “pouring in, storing”, a looser sense than “pour out” elsewhere. Balaγad is the plural known as “towns”, but the Ming here is 庫每 “storehouses”, so I read “treasuries”. Sakiγ̇uluγ̇a is saki- “guard” + causative -γ̇ul- + a hortative in -γ̇a (Ming 敎守咱), “let us have it guarded”.

morph.gloss: aγ̇urasun — length of cloth, bolt of silk (noun; stem as printed; uncertain) [段疋]
sükes — silver ingot(s) (noun; the final -s perhaps a plural) [銀錠]
žebe — weapon, gear (noun; not the name Jebe) [器︀械]
saṅγ̇ — granary, storehouse (noun; stem uncertain, read from the Ming 倉每) [倉每]
tüsür- — to pour (verb; here, from the Ming 注着, 'pour in, store') [注着]
balaγasun — town, city (noun; but the Ming here is 庫每 'storehouses', so 'treasuries') [庫每]
saki- — to guard, keep watch (verb) [敎守咱]
hortative: 'let us …' (first person plural, back-vowel form)

sentences.t: Žüg žüg-eče balaγačin amučin ilγažu sakiγ̇ultuγai.
sentences.l: Place place-from town-keepers grain-keepers picking-out, let-them-be-made-to-guard.
sentences.i: Let the keepers of the towns and the keepers of the grain be picked out from each region and set to guard them.
sentences.n: Balaγačin (Ming 管城的) is “town-keeper”: balaγasun + agent -čin. Amučin (Ming 管米的) is “grain-keeper”; amu “rice, grain” is read from the Ming 米. The Ming here glosses balaγa- as 城 “town”, though it glossed balaγad above as 庫 “storehouse”; the two senses may be one word. Ilγažu is “picking out” (Ming 揀着). Sakiγ̇ultuγai is saki- + causative + the optative -tuγai, “let them be made to guard”.

morph.gloss: balaγasun — town, city (noun; the stem balaγa- before -čin) [管城的]
amu — rice, grain (noun; stem read from the Ming 米) [管米的]
ilγa- — to pick out, separate (verb) [選揀着]
saki- — to guard, keep watch (verb) [敎守者︀]

sentences.t: Basa ulus irgen-e nutuγ usu qubijažu ögüje.
sentences.l: Again people people-to camp water dividing, let-us-give.
sentences.i: Again, let us give the people pasture and water, dividing them out.
sentences.n: Ulus irgen-e is “to the realm and people”, the two nouns read as one idea (Ming 百姓 百姓行). Nutuγ is the camping ground, home pasture (Ming 營盤); usu is usun “water” with the n lost in print. Qubijažu is qubija- “divide” (stem inferred from the Ming 分着) + converb -žu.

morph.gloss: usun — water (noun; the final n lost in print) [水]
qubija- — to divide, share out (verb; stem inferred from the Ming) [分着]
hortative: 'let us …' (first person plural, front-vowel form)

sentences.t: Nutuγ nutulaγ̇uluquj-a miṅγad miṅγad-ača nutuγ̇učin ilγažu γarγaγ̇asu bolqu-ju.
sentences.l: Camp camp-for-making thousands thousands-from camp-managers picking-out, if-sending-out, will-it-be-fitting?
sentences.i: For the laying out of camps, if we pick camp-managers from every thousand and send them out, will that serve?
sentences.n: Nutulaγ̇uluquj-a is nutula- “make a camp” + causative -γ̇ul- + participle -qu + a dative-locative -a with a linking j (Ming 做營盤 行), “for the making of camps”. Nutuγ̇učin is the camp-manager (nutuγ + agent). Γarγaγ̇asu is “if (we) send out”: γar- + causative + -γ̇asu. Bolqu-ju is bol- “be” + participle -qu + -ju, which I take as a question particle (the glossary's guess); the Ming 中 麽有 (“will it do?”) supports a question.

morph.gloss: nutula- — to make camp (nutuγ 'camp' + verb-maker -la-; Ming 做營盤) (verb) [做營盤 行]
dative-locative: 'for, to' (after a participle; the j is a linking sound)
ilγa- — to pick out, separate (verb) [選揀着]
bol- — to be, become, do (verb) [中 麽有]

sentences.t: Basa Čül γažar-a göreġesün-eče busu ülü amui.
sentences.l: Again Čül land-in wild-beasts-from other not is.
sentences.i: Again: in the land of Chül there is nothing but wild beasts.
sentences.n: Čül is a place name (Ming 地名); the Ming says only that, and I cannot place it. Göreġesün-eče busu ülü amui is “from wild beasts, other, not is”: göreġesün (Ming 野獸) “wild beast, game”, the ablative as “apart from”, busu “other”, ülü “not”, amui “is”. So the land has only wild animals, no people.

morph.gloss: Čül — Chül, a place name (Ming gives only 地名; the place is not known to me) [地名]
göreġesün — wild beast, game (noun; Ming 野獸) [野獸行]
ülü — not (negates a converb or participle) [不]

sentences.t: Irgen-e aγ̇uj-a saγud Čanai, Uiγ̇urtai qojar nutuγ̇učin-i teriġüležü Čül-ün quduγ̇ud eriġülžü qašituγai.
sentences.l: People-to wide-in some Čanai, Uiγ̇urtai two camp-managers-(obj) at-the-head-being Čül-of wells making-seek, let-them-line.
sentences.i: To ease things for the people, let Chanai and Uighurtai, the two, heading the camp-managers, have wells dug in Chül and lined.
sentences.n: The first clause is doubtful: aγ̇uj-a is read from the Ming 寬行 “to width, roominess”, and saγud (Ming 些 “a little”) is unexplained (it may be from saγu- “sit”); I give only the sense “to ease things for the people”. Uiγ̇urtai (Ming 人名) is a man's name, perhaps Uiγ̇ur “Uighur” + -tai. Teriġüležü is teriġü “head” + -le- + converb, “being at the head”. Qojar nutuγ̇učin-i could also be “the two camp-managers” (accusative) in apposition to the names; I read the two as the leaders and the camp-managers as the men they head. Eriġülžü is eri- “seek” + causative (Ming 敎掘着, “have dug”); qašituγai (Ming 甃) I read as “let them be lined” with stone, tentatively.

morph.gloss: aγ̇uj — breadth, roominess (stem inferred from the Ming 寬 'wide'; uncertain) [寬行]
saγud — some, a little (Ming 些; the word is uncertain and may be a form of saγu- 'sit') [些]
Čanai — Chanai, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
Uiγ̇urtai — Uighurtai, a man's name (Ming 人名; perhaps Uiγ̇ur 'Uighur' + -tai 'having') [人名]
nutuγ — camp, pasture (noun) [管營盤的 行]
Čül — Chül, a place name (Ming 地名) [地名的]
quduγ — well (noun; the Ming 井) [井每]
eri- — to seek, look for (verb; here the Ming reads 敎掘着, 'have dug') [敎掘着]
qaši- — to line (a well) with stone or brick (stem inferred from the Ming 甃; uncertain) (verb) [甃者︀]

sentences.t: Basa bida elčin qaγ̇ulurun ulus bitüġülün qaγ̇ulγamui.
sentences.l: Again we envoys when-rushing people making-go-along, make-run,
sentences.i: Again: when envoys rush, we make the people go along the road and run,
sentences.n: The Ming glosses qaγ̇ulurun 奔時 “when rushing”, not the 征時 “when campaigning” of other parts. Bitüġülün (Ming 沿着 “along”) I take as “making them go along (the route)”, that is, the people are pressed to serve the road; this is a guess from the Ming. Qaγ̇ulγamui is qaγ̇ul- + causative -γa- + present -mui, “makes run”. Bida is “we” (inclusive, Ming 咱). Shiratori puts no stop here; I cut it here for reading.

morph.gloss: bida — we (inclusive: you and I; first-person plural pronoun) [咱]
qaγ̇ul- — to rush, run (verb; here the Ming reads 奔) [奔時]
bitü- — to go along, take around (stem uncertain; Ming 沿着 'along') (verb) [敎沿着]

sentences.t: qaγ̇ulqun elčin-ü ba jabudal udaγ̇an bi.
sentences.l: rushers envoys-of also going slow is.
sentences.i: and even the journeys of the envoys who rush are slow.
sentences.n: Qaγ̇ulqun is qaγ̇ul- + a participle -qun, “those who rush” (Ming 奔的每); elčin-ü is “of the envoys” (Ming 使臣的); ba is “also” (Ming 也). Jabudal (Ming 行程) “journey, going” and udaγ̇an (Ming 遲) “slow” give the complaint: the present arrangement burdens the people and is slow.

morph.gloss: participle: 'those who …' (the Ming 的每 marks the plural; uncertain)
bi — is, exists (verb; perhaps a short form of bü-) [有]

sentences.t: Ulus irgen-e ba žobolaṅ bi.
sentences.l: Realm people-to also hardship is.
sentences.i: And the people, too, suffer hardship.
sentences.n: Žobolaṅ (Ming 生受) is “hardship, suffering”, a noun related to žoban “toil”; bi “is”. Ulus irgen-e ba is “to the realm and people, also”.

morph.gloss: žobolaṅ — hardship, suffering (noun; related to žoban 'toil'; Ming 生受) [生受]
bi — is, exists (verb; perhaps a short form of bü-) [有]

sentences.t: Edöġe bida oγ̇oγ̇ata orosiγ̇ulun žüg žüg-ün miṅγad miṅγad-ača žamčin ulaγ̇ačin γarγažu saγ̇urid saγ̇urid žam talbižu
sentences.l: Now we altogether making-settle, place place-of thousands thousands-from post-keepers grooms taking-out, posts posts stations setting-up,
sentences.i: Now we, all together giving things a fixed form, drawing out post-households and grooms from the thousands of each region, and setting up a station at every post,
sentences.n: Oγ̇oγ̇ata (Ming 一發) is “altogether”; orosiγ̇ulun (Ming 定體 “fixed form”) I read as “making settled”, from an inferred orosi-. Žamčin (Ming 站戶) is žam “post-station” + agent -čin, a post-household; ulaγ̇ačin (Ming 馬夫) is a groom (ulaγ̇a “relay horse” + -čin). Saγ̇urid saγ̇urid is “post by post” (each seat, Ming 坐每 坐每). Talbižu is “setting, posting” (Ming 放着). There is no “let us” in the form: orosiγ̇ulun is a converb, and the verb of the whole chain is the question that ends the next unit. The long chain of converbs is broken at the stations; it resumes with the envoys.

sentences.t: elčin-i qadaγa ügei ulus(i)-jar ülü bituγ̇ulun žam(i)-jar qaγ̇ulγaγ̇asu bolqu-ju.
sentences.l: envoys-(obj) urgent-matter without people-by not making-go-along, post-by if-making-run, will-it-be-fitting?
sentences.i: would it serve, when there is no urgent business, to send the envoys by the posts and not by way of the people?
sentences.n: Elčin-i is the envoys as object (Ming 使臣行). Qadaγa ügei (Ming 緊要事 無) is “without urgent business”. Ulus(i)-jar and žam(i)-jar are instrumentals, “by the people” and “by the post” (the (i) is Shiratori's linking vowel). Bituγ̇ulun (Ming 敎治着, “having them governed”) I take to be the same word as bitüġülün in the earlier unit (there Ming 敎沿着, “along”; 治 and 沿 look alike, so one is probably a copyist's slip), in the same frame: the people are made to go along the route, or the posts are. So “not making (them) go along by way of the people”. The Ming 治 is noted, not followed; uncertain. Bolqu-ju is the same question tag as before.

sentences.t: Ede üiles-i Čanai, Bolγadar qojar uqažu bidan-a duradγaγ̇asu
sentences.l: These matters-(obj) Čanai, Bolγadar two understanding us-to if-they-raise
sentences.i: If Chanai and Bolqadar, the two, having considered these matters, bring them to us,
sentences.n: Üiles-i is üile “matter” + plural -s + accusative -i, “these matters” (Ming 事每 行). Uqažu is “understanding, perceiving” (Ming 省着). Bidan-a is “to us” (bida + -n- + dative-locative -a; the Ming 俺行 reads “we” as exclusive though the sense is Ögödei's “us”). Duradγaγ̇asu is duradγa- (Ming 提說 “mention”) + -γ̇asu, “if they bring it up”.

sentences.t: žöb aqu-ju keġen sedkižü Čaγ̇adai aqa medetügei.
sentences.l: right is-it? saying, thinking, Čaγ̇adai elder-brother let-know.
sentences.i: thinking ‘Is it right?’, let my elder brother Cha'adai be the judge.
sentences.n: Žöb aqu-ju is “right — is it?” (Ming 是 有麽), with -ju the question tag; keġen “saying” closes the thought (Ming 麽道), and sedkižü is “thinking” (Ming 想着). Who thinks is not clear: I read Ögödei. Medetügei is mede- “know” + optative, “let him know” (Ming 知者); I give “be the judge” for the sense. Another reading is that the two men, not Ögödei, are the ones asking.

sentences.t: Ede ügülegdekün üiles žokiqui böġesü žöbšijeġesü Čaγ̇adai aqāča boltuγai"
sentences.l: These spoken matters fitting if-being, if-approving, Čaγ̇adai elder-brother-from let-it-be"
sentences.i: If these matters that have been spoken are fitting, and he approves, let it be done on the word of my elder brother Cha'adai.”
sentences.n: Ügülegdekün is ügüle- “speak” + passive -gde- + participle -kün, “what is spoken” (Ming 說的每). Žokiqui böġesü (Ming 宣 有呵) is “if it is fitting”; žöbšijeġesü (Ming 道是呵) “if he agrees”. Aqāča is aqa + ablative -ača, “from elder brother”; the Ming 兄行 … 做者 is “let it be done by (to) elder brother Cha'adai”; “on the word of” in the English keeps the ablative “from”. The closing mark after boltuγai ends Ögödei's speech, begun at Čiṅgis.

sentences.t: keġežü ileġesü Čaγ̇adai aqa asaγču ilegsen
sentences.l: saying, if-sending, Čaγ̇adai elder-brother asking, the-sent-one
sentences.i: Having said this, he sent a man; and the man sent asked elder brother Cha'adai,
sentences.n: Keġežü is “saying” (Ming 說着); ileġesü is ile- “send” + the conditional -ġesü, “if, when he sends” (the Ming has 去 “go”). Asaγču is “asking” (Ming 問着), and ilegsen is the past participle, “the one sent” (Ming 去了的). I take the messenger as the subject of the next unit's irežüġüi; another construction is possible.

sentences.t: "ede ele üiles-i bügüde-ji žöbšiježü tein böġed kitügei" keġežü irežüġüi.
sentences.l: "these indeed matters all-(obj) approving so being let-it-be-done" saying, came.
sentences.i: “All these matters are approved; so let it be done,” he said, and came.
sentences.n: This is Cha'adai's answer, which the messenger brings back; the opening mark is Shiratori's. Bügüde-ji is “all” as object (Ming 都 行); žöbšiježü is “approving” (Ming 道是着); tein böġed (Ming 那般 便) “so, thereupon”, böġed being an uncertain ending. Kitügei is ki- “do” + optative, “let it be done”. Keġežü irežüġüi is “saying, came”: ire- + the narrative past -žüġüi (Ming 說着 來了有).

sentences.n: Ügüležü irerün is “speaking, coming” (Ming 說着 來), the two converbs in the pattern used elsewhere for a message delivered; I read that Cha'adai's message is carried, not that he himself comes.

sentences.t: "Bi endēče žamud esergü bariduγ̇ulsuγai.
sentences.l: "I from-here posts to-meet let-me-have-joined.
sentences.i: “From this end I shall have the post-stations set to meet and join up with yours.
sentences.n: Bi is “I” here (Ming 我), not the verb “is”. Endēče is ene “this” + the ablative with a long vowel, “from here” (Ming 自這裏). Esergü (Ming 迎着) is “to meet, facing”. Bariduγ̇ulsuγai is bari- “take hold” + -du- (reciprocal) + causative -γ̇ul- + the first-person optative -suγai (Ming 相接我, “let me have them join”). The “yours” is my addition for the sense.

sentences.l: Again from-here Batu-to envoy let-me-send.
sentences.i: And from here I shall send an envoy to Batu:
sentences.n: Batu-dur is Batu + dative-locative (Ming 人名 行), “to Batu”. Ilesügei is ile- “send” + the first-person optative -sügei (Ming 敎去我), “let me send”. The colon is mine: the envoy's message follows.

sentences.t: Batu ber esergü žamud(i)-jan barildγ̇ul- tuγai"
sentences.l: Batu also to-meet posts-his-own let-them-be-made-to-join"
sentences.i: let Batu, too, have his own post-stations meet them and join up.”
sentences.n: The word barildγ̇ul-tuγai is broken at the line end in Shiratori (barildγ̇ul- / tuγai), and I keep it as two printed words. It is bari- + reciprocal -ldu- + causative -γ̇ul- + optative -tuγai, “let them be made to join”. Žamud(i)-jan is “his own post-stations” (žam + plural -ud + the reflexive-possessive -(i)jan; Ming 站每自的行). Ber (Ming 也) is “also”. The closing mark ends the message to Batu.

sentences.l: having-said, again speaking, coming:
sentences.i: Having said this, he again came speaking:

sentences.t: "Bügüdēče žamud talbiγ̇ulqu üile žöb(e)-eče žöb duradγažuγ̇ui" keġežü irežüġüi.
sentences.l: "all-from posts setting-up matter right-from right (you)-have-mentioned" saying, came.
sentences.i: “Of everything, the setting up of the post-stations is the most right that you have raised,” he said as he came.
sentences.n: Žöb(e)-eče žöb (Ming 是行 是) is literally “from right, right”; I take it as a superlative, “rightest of all”, which is my reading. Bügüdēče is “from all” (Ming 都行); talbiγ̇ulqu üile is “the matter of setting up (posts)”: talbi- + causative + participle -qu. Duradγažuγ̇ui is “has brought up” (Ming 提說了). Keġežü irežüġüi, “saying, came”, as above. This closes the exchange with Cha'adai.

žöb — right, proper (the (e) is Shiratori's; Ming 是行) [是行]

sentences.l: From-there Ögödei Qaγan, saying:
sentences.i: Thereupon Ögödei Qahan spoke:
sentences.n: Tendēče is tende “there” + the ablative with a long vowel (Ming 自那裏), “from there, thereupon”. A new section: Ögödei now addresses the assembled princes and officers. The speech opens at the next word.

sentences.t: "Čaγ̇adai aqa Batu teriġüten baraγ̇un γar-un köġüd aqa-nar deġü-ner bürin;
sentences.l: "Čaγ̇adai elder-brother Batu heading right hand's princes elder-brothers younger-brothers all;
sentences.i: “All the princes of the right hand, elder brothers and younger brothers, headed by my elder brother Cha'adai and Batu;
sentences.n: Teriġüten is teriġü “head” + the plural possessive -ten, “those having X at their head” (Ming 等 “and the rest”); the form is uncertain. Baraγ̇un γar-un (Ming 右 手的) is “of the right hand”, the right wing; with žeġün “left” and γol “centre” below it gives the three divisions of the realm. Köġüd is köġün “son” + -d, “princes” (Ming 大王每); aqa-nar and deġü-ner are the plurals “elder brothers” and “younger brothers”. Opening mark: Shiratori's.

sentences.t: köġüd γol-un ökid küriged tümed-ün miṅγad-un žaγ̇ud-un harbad-un nojad büri-jer žöbšiježüġüi.
sentences.l: princes centre-of daughters sons-in-law ten-thousands-of thousands-of hundreds-of tens-of officers all-by agreed.
sentences.i: the princes of the centre, the daughters and sons-in-law, and all the officers of the ten-thousands, the thousands, the hundreds and the tens: all have agreed.
sentences.n: Γol-un (Ming 在內) is “of the centre”. Ökid and küriged are “daughters” and “sons-in-law” with the plural -d (the stem küregen loses its n). Tümed-ün, miṅγad-un, žaγ̇ud-un, harbad-un are the plural genitives of the four ranks, “of the ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens”, which the Ming reads as the commanders of each (萬戶的, 千戶的, 百戶的, 十戶的). Büri-jer (Ming 衆) is “all together”. Žöbšiježüġüi is “agreed” (Ming 道是了).

sentences.t: Žöbšijerün dalai-jin Qaγan-(n)u sülen-e hon-dur sürüg-ün nigen šilekü irge γarγaγ̇asu jaγ̇un bi.
sentences.l: Agreeing, sea-of Qaγan's broth-for year-in herd-of one two-year wether if-taking-out, what is?
sentences.i: When they had agreed: for the broth of the Qahan of all within the seas, if one two-year-old wether is taken from each flock every year, what is there in that?
sentences.n: Žöbšijerün is “when agreeing” (Ming 道是時). Dalai-jin Qaγan-(n)u is “of the sea-Qahan” (Ming 海內的 皇帝 的), the Qahan of the world; Ögödei speaks of himself so. Sülen-e, the broth, is the levy as in the earlier part of this section. Irge is “wether” (Ming 羯羊). Jaγ̇un bi (Ming 甚 有) is “what is there?”, a rhetorical question: it is no burden.

žarliγ — command, decree (noun; the (i) is Shiratori's) [聖旨 依着]

sentences.t: hon hon-dur sülen-e sürüg-eče nigen šilekü irge žaγ̇un qonid-ača nigen žusaγ qonin γarγaγ̇ulba.
sentences.l: year year-in broth-for herd-from one two-year wether, hundred sheep-from one yearling sheep he-had-taken-out.
sentences.i: he had one two-year-old wether drawn from the flock every year for the broth, and one yearling sheep from every hundred sheep.
sentences.n: Hon hon-dur (Ming 年 年裏) is “year, in the year”, that is, “every year”. Γarγaγ̇ulba is γar- “go out” + causative -γa- + causative -γ̇ul- + past -ba, “had drawn out, had levied” (Ming 敎出了). The levy is the one proposed in §279, now put into effect by decree.

morph.gloss: sülen — soup, broth (noun; here, I think, the levy for the ruler's table) [湯行]
šilekü — two-year-old (of an animal) (adjective; reading from the Ming 二歲) [二歲]
žusaγ — yearling, one-year-old (of an animal) (noun; Ming 一歲) [一歲]

sentences.t: Geġüd γarγaγ̇ulžu unuγ̇učin saγ̇ulba.
sentences.l: Mares having-had-taken-out, mare-keepers he-had-seated.
sentences.i: He had mares drawn out and mare-keepers installed.
sentences.n: Geġüd is the “mares” of §279; unuγ̇učin is the “mare-keeper” (Ming 放乳馬的). Saγ̇ulba is saγu- “sit” + causative -l- + past -ba (Ming 敎坐了, “made sit”), which I give as “installed”; the Ming's “seated” could be literal.

morph.gloss: geġü — mare kept for milking (noun; Ming (騍)馬每 'mares'; reading uncertain) [(騍)馬每]
unuγ̇učin — keeper of milk-mares, mare-keeper (Ming 放乳馬的; stem inferred) [放(乳)馬的]

sentences.t: Unuγ̇učin balaγačin amučin γarγaγ̇ulba.
sentences.l: Mare-keepers, town-keepers, grain-keepers he-had-taken-out.
sentences.i: He had the mare-keepers, the town-keepers and the grain-keepers drawn out.
sentences.n: These are the three offices named in §279 (balaγačin, amučin as above). γarγaγ̇ulba is again “had drawn out”, which I keep as “had drawn out” (that is, drafted into the office; the Ming has 敎出了, “had brought out”).

morph.gloss: unuγ̇učin — keeper of milk-mares, mare-keeper (Ming 放乳馬的; stem inferred) [放(乳)馬的]
balaγasun — town, city (noun; the stem balaγa- before -čin) [管城的]
amu — rice, grain (noun; stem read from the Ming 米) [管米的]

sentences.t: žamčin ulaγ̇ačin-i γarγaγ̇ulžu
sentences.l: Post-keepers grooms-(obj) having-had-taken-out,
sentences.i: Having had the post-households and grooms drawn out,
sentences.n: Žamčin and ulaγ̇ačin-i are the post-households and grooms of §279, the second with the accusative -i (Ming 馬夫行). Γarγaγ̇ulžu is the converb of the same causative as above.

morph.gloss: žam — post-station, relay (noun; Ming 站) [站戶]
ulaγ̇a — post-horse, relay horse (noun; stem read from the Ming 馬夫) [馬夫行]

sentences.t: saγ̇urin saγ̇urid-un γažar čaγlaγ̇lžu žam talbiγ̇ulurun
sentences.l: post posts'-of land having-had-weighed, station when-setting-up,
sentences.i: weighing the ground for each post, and, when he set up the stations,
sentences.n: Saγ̇urin saγ̇urid-un γažar is literally “post, of the posts, land”, which I read as “the ground for each post”. Čaγlaγ̇lžu (Ming 斟酌着) is čaγla- “weigh, judge” + causative + converb, printed with the vowel dropped, so a slip or a contraction. Talbiγ̇ulurun is “when (he) set up” (Ming 敎放時): talbi- + causative + the converb of time -run.

morph.gloss: saγ̇urin — seat, post, station (noun; from saγ̇u- 'sit') [坐]
čaγla- — to weigh, judge, reckon (verb) [斟酌着]
talbi- — to set down, post (verb) [敎放時]

sentences.t: Aračan, Toqučar qojar-i žasaγ̇ulžu
sentences.l: Aračan, Toqučar two-(obj) having-had-set-in-order
sentences.i: having had Arachan and Toquchar, the two, put it in order,
sentences.n: Aračan and Toqučar are men's names (Ming 人名 each); qojar-i is “the two” as object (Ming 兩箇行). Žasaγ̇ulžu is žasa- “set in order” + causative + converb (Ming 敎整治着), “having had it arranged”. The object of the arranging, the stations, is carried over from the previous unit.

morph.gloss: Aračan — Arachan, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
Toqučar — Toquchar, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
qojar — two, the pair (numeral) [兩箇 行]
žasa- — to prepare, set in order (verb) [敎整治着]

sentences.t: žam nigen saγ̇urin-dur qorin ulaγ̇ačin bolγaba.
sentences.l: station one post-in twenty groom he-made.
sentences.i: he made twenty grooms for each single post.
sentences.n: Žam nigen saγ̇urin-dur is “station, one post, in”, so “at each post”; qorin ulaγ̇ačin is “twenty grooms”, and bolγaba is bol- “become” + causative -γa- + past, “made them” (Ming 敎做了). Shiratori prints this and the next unit as two sentences that say nearly the same; I follow him.

morph.gloss: saγ̇urin — seat, post, station (noun) [坐 裏]
ulaγ̇a — post-horse, relay horse (noun; stem read from the Ming 馬夫) [馬夫]

sentences.t: saγ̇urin tutum- dur qoriγ̇ad ulaγ̇ačin bolγaba.
sentences.l: post each-in twenty-each groom he-made.
sentences.i: At every post he made twenty grooms apiece.
sentences.n: Tutum- and dur are one word broken at the line end in Shiratori (tutum-dur), “in each”, which I keep as two printed words. Qoriγ̇ad (Ming 每二十箇) is “twenty each”; the ending is tentative.

morph.gloss: saγ̇urin — seat, post, station (noun; from saγ̇u- 'sit') [坐]
tutum — each, every one (pronoun or adjective; printed with a hyphen at the line end) [每]
-dur — dative-locative: 'at, in' (suffix; the second half of tutum-dur, broken at the line end; Ming 裏) [裏]
distributive: 'twenty each' (tentative; the n of qorin is lost)
ulaγ̇a — post-horse, relay horse (noun; stem read from the Ming 馬夫) [馬夫]

sentences.t: ulaγ̇an-u aγtas šiġüsün-ü qonid saγ̇alin geġüd teregen-dür kölkü hüker terged
sentences.l: Post-horses'-of geldings, ration-of sheep, milking mares, cart-in yoking oxen, carts,
sentences.i: “The geldings of the post-horses, the sheep for rations, the mares for milking, the oxen to be yoked to carts, and the carts,
sentences.n: A list with no verb: ulaγ̇an-u aγtas (Ming 鋪馬的 騸馬每) “the geldings of the post-horses”, šiġüsün-ü qonid (Ming 分例的 羊每) “the sheep of the ration”, saγ̇alin geġüd “the mares to be milked”, teregen-dür kölkü hüker (Ming 車裏 駕的 牛) “the oxen yoked to carts”, and terged “carts”. The next unit says what is to happen if they are short. Shiratori prints a closing mark at boltuγai (the end of the penalty clauses) with no opening mark before it, the speech that began at Čaγ̇adai having already been closed at žöbšiježüġüi; I supply the opening here, at the start of the decree's wording, in the English only. Where exactly it begins is my guess.

morph.gloss: ulaγ̇a — post-horse, relay horse (noun) [鋪馬 的]
šiġüsün — ration, allowance (noun; Ming 分例) [分例的]
geġü — mare kept for milking (noun; Ming (騍)馬每 'mares'; reading uncertain) [(騍)馬每]
tergen — cart, wagon (noun; printed teregen-) [車裏]
kölge- — to yoke, harness (verb; printed kölkü, the ge apparently dropped) [駕的]
tergen — cart, wagon (noun; terge- before the plural) [車每]

sentences.t: endēče bidan-ača kemlegsen kem-eče oqor bugi dutaγ̇uluγ̇asu orγol(i)-jar qaγas aldaltan boltuγai.
sentences.l: from-here us-from fixed limit-from short rope if-made-lacking, neck-by split penalty-having let-be.
sentences.i: if any of these is left short of the limit fixed by us from here, even by a short rope's length, let those responsible be cleft by the neck and forfeit.
sentences.n: Kemlegsen kem-eče is “from the limit fixed” (kemle- “set a limit” + past participle; Ming 限定了的 限行); bidan-ača is “from us”. Oqor bugi (Ming 短 繩) is “a short rope”; I read it as the smallest shortfall, which is a guess. Dutaγ̇uluγ̇asu is “if (they) are made lacking” (Ming 缺少了呵). The penalty is uncertain: orγol(i)-jar (Ming 惱項敎, “by the nape and neck”), qaγas (Ming 劈破 “split open”) and aldaltan (Ming 斷沒, “cut off and confiscated”) point to a cleaving and forfeiture, but the exact sense of each is not settled.

morph.gloss: ene — this (demonstrative; stem end- before a case ending) [自這裏]
stem-final n before a case ending
kemle- — to fix a limit, set a measure (from kem 'limit') (verb) [限定了的]
bugi — rope, cord (noun; Ming 繩; reading uncertain) [繩]
dutaγ̇u- — to lack, be wanting (verb) [缺少了呵]
orγol — nape, neck (stem inferred from the Ming 惱項 'nape and neck'; uncertain) (noun; the (i) is Shiratori's) [惱項敎]
instrumental: 'by, at' (the Ming 敎 marks the means)
qaγas — split, cleft (Ming 劈破 'split open'; reading uncertain) [劈破]
aldal — fault, penalty, forfeiture (noun; Ming 斷沒 'cut off and confiscated') [斷沒(的每)]
plural possessive: 'those having, those subject to'
optative: 'let it be, may it be' (back-vowel form)

sentences.t: Qalbuγa kegesün dutaγ̇uluγ̇asu qabar qaγas aldaltan boltuγai" keġen žarliγ bolba.
sentences.l: Spoon-piece, spokes if-made-lacking, nose split penalty-having let-be" saying decree he-made.
sentences.i: If the spoon-pieces or the spokes are left lacking, let those responsible be cleft at the nose and forfeit,” so saying, he issued it as a decree.
sentences.n: Qalbuγa (Ming 匙般, “spoon-like”) and kegesün (Ming 車輻, “spokes”) are parts of a cart; qalbuγa is a guess at some spoon-shaped piece, which I cannot name. Qabar is “nose” (Ming 鼻子). The closing mark after boltuγai is the one that closes the decree's wording (see the note on the list of goods). Keġen žarliγ bolba is “saying (so), the decree became” (Ming 麽道 聖旨 做了): the rule is issued as an imperial decree.

morph.gloss: qalbuγa — spoon, spoon-shaped piece (Ming 匙般 'spoon-like'; here apparently a cart fitting) [匙般]
kegesün — spoke(s) of a wheel (Ming 車輻) [車輻]
dutaγ̇u- — to lack, be wanting (verb) [缺少了呵]
qaγas — split, cleft (Ming 劈破 'split open'; reading uncertain) [劈破]
aldal — fault, penalty, forfeiture (noun; Ming 斷沒 'cut off and confiscated') [斷沒(的每)]
plural possessive: 'those having, those subject to'
optative: 'let it be, may it be' (back-vowel form)
